evidence_quotes.quote: From the borehole, the water is pumped into a large communal reservoir, from which every member of the community can access it for personal and pastoral use.

while the government provides a basic supply of infrastructure (coverage), the infrastructure is then handed over to local communities, which are responsible for covering operation, maintenance, and, later, full ownership costs.

To collect the necessary financial means, communities were advised to agree on water payment schemes that reflect the amount of water households use and the economic benefits they draw from water use.

To understand the economic implications of water-associated costs, we conducted a monthly survey on household expenditures with eighty-one households for ten months between February 2015 and January 2016.

In a social situation where many people are poor and money is very scarce, many households find it hard to afford water. As a consequence, some withdraw money for water from other economic activities. Others cannot pay at all.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural household and community access to groundwater pumped from communal boreholes for personal and pastoral use in northwestern Namibia.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies Criterion 2 under BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Plain wording: examines institutional, legal, and governance reforms under Namibia's 1993 Water and Sanitation Policy (WASP) and 1997 Cabinet Memorandum introducing Community-Based Management (CBM). Narrow 2026-10-13 reading: directly examines tariff and cost-recovery rules, ownership-transfer agreements shifting full operational/maintenance/ownership responsibilities from the state to local Water Point Committees, per-livestock water fee rules and monthly household diesel-contribution rules, and local compliance/enforcement governing communal water access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains original mixed-methods empirical data collected from 2010 onward in southern Kunene (Fransfontein and ‡Khoadi ||Hôas), combining ethnographic participant observation, qualitative interviews, policy document analysis, and a 10-month household expenditure survey of 81 households (Feb 2015–Jan 2016).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household water affordability and access-related outcomes, including monthly/annual household water expenditures (averaging N$99/month or N$991/year), crowding out of food/health/education spending, inability of poor households to pay diesel fees, withdrawal of wealthy households into private storage tanks, exclusion, and water-point conflicts.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (households and rural pastoral communities in Fransfontein and ‡Khoadi ||Hôas, Kunene region, Namibia; n=81 households in the monthly expenditure survey), exposure (CBM cost-recovery, ownership devolution, and water pricing/diesel contribution rules), outcome (affordability burden, non-payment, exclusion, and social conflict), and mixed-methods ethnographic/survey study design are all clearly specified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Mixed-methods empirical study combining ethnographic participant observation, qualitative interviews, policy document analysis, and a 10-month longitudinal household expenditure survey.
population_and_sample: Rural pastoralist communities and households in Fransfontein and ‡Khoadi ||Hôas conservancy, southern Kunene region, northwestern Namibia, including a 10-month longitudinal survey of 81 households (February 2015 to January 2016) alongside multi-site ethnographic fieldwork and interviews.
exposure: Post-apartheid Namibian Community-Based Management (CBM) water policy (1993 Water and Sanitation Policy and 1997 Cabinet Memorandum) mandating state subsidy withdrawal, handover of borehole infrastructure ownership to Water Point Committees, and household cost-recovery tariff/diesel-contribution rules.
outcome: Household water affordability and expenditure burden (N$99/month or N$991/year on average), inability to pay and rule noncompliance among poor households, elite opt-out via private tanks, exclusion, and local social conflict over water access.
rationale: This mixed-methods empirical study meets all inclusion criteria (c1–c6). It examines rural household and community water access in northwestern Namibia (c1) under legal and administrative reforms (1993 WASP and 1997 Cabinet Memorandum) that devolved water-point ownership and imposed cost-recovery and tariff/diesel-contribution rules directly governing access (c2 under both plain and narrow rule-type readings). Using ethnographic fieldwork, interviews, and a 10-month survey of 81 households (c3, c5), the study documents severe household affordability burdens, non-payment, exclusion, and conflict resulting from the cost-recovery regime (c4), and is published in English (c6).
